name: Threat Modelling for Legal AI
title: Threat Modelling for Legal AI
answer: Threat modelling for legal AI is the structured practice of identifying, ranking, and documenting plausible failure and attack paths in AI systems used for legal work, such as document review, legal research, contract analysis, and client communication. It covers confidentiality of privileged material, integrity of legal advice and citations, availability of tools during deadlines, and manipulation of model outputs through prompt injection or poisoned training data. The scope includes both the AI model and the surrounding application, data pipelines, access controls, and human review steps. It is used to decide which controls to build or buy before a system is deployed and to revisit those decisions when models, data, or use cases change.

sections.body: Threat modelling for legal AI is the structured practice of identifying, ranking, and documenting plausible failure and attack paths in AI systems used for legal work, such as document review, legal research, contract analysis, and client communication. It covers confidentiality of privileged material, integrity of legal advice and citations, availability of tools during deadlines, and manipulation of model outputs through prompt injection or poisoned training data. The scope includes both the AI model and the surrounding application, data pipelines, access controls, and human review steps. It is used to decide which controls to build or buy before a system is deployed and to revisit those decisions when models, data, or use cases change.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The systems being modelled typically run on a mix of cloud-hosted large language models, retrieval pipelines over firm documents, and internal applications that connect to practice management, e-discovery, and billing platforms. Threat modelling work itself is usually done in structured workshops, diagramming tools, and risk registers, not inside the AI runtime. The infrastructure under review includes model endpoints, vector databases, document stores, API gateways, identity providers, and logging or audit systems. Because legal AI often handles privileged and personally identifiable data, the infrastructure boundaries between tenant data, model provider processing, and firm-controlled storage are a central focus.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by assembling a description of the system, identifying assets such as client confidences, work product, and court filings, and then walking through threat scenarios using frameworks like STRIDE or attack trees. Participants include security staff, legal operations, IT, and the lawyers who will rely on the tool, because the most serious failures are often misuse or overreliance rather than a technical exploit. Each scenario is rated by likelihood and impact, with particular attention to prompt injection, data leakage between matters, hallucinated citations, and unauthorized access through weak API keys or shared accounts. The output is a prioritized list of controls, test cases, and monitoring checks rather than a one-time compliance document.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in legal AI threat modelling turn on duties of confidentiality, competence, and supervision, along with data protection and export control rules that vary by jurisdiction. The site tracks 142 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, which reflects the live dispute risk around training data, model outputs, and vendor terms. Threat modelling records should show who reviewed a model's output, what data it was allowed to see, and how incidents will be reported to clients, insurers, or regulators. Provenance matters because a model's training data, fine-tuning, retrieval sources, and prompt history all affect whether an output can be trusted or defended. No part of the process should be treated as legal advice to a client; it is an internal control practice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Threat modelling for legal AI is moving from ad hoc security reviews toward continuous, evidence-based assurance tied to model versions, retrieval corpora, and actual usage logs. As courts and bar regulators issue guidance on AI use, firms will need to show that they modelled threats before deployment and updated the model after incidents or material changes. The practice is likely to merge with vendor due diligence, red-teaming, and audit trails that record prompt, retrieved source, and human review for high-stakes work. Over time, threat models may become machine-readable artifacts that feed automated policy checks and incident response, but the core judgment will remain with lawyers and security staff who understand the matter at hand.
